newsitem.title: USA: US Fed policy seen pushing dlr/mark past 1994 peak.
newsitem.headline: US Fed policy seen pushing dlr/mark past 1994 peak.

text.p: Dollar/mark is surging to levels not seen since February 1994 and -- unlike three years ago -- the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy won't derail this rally, according to market experts.

"The Fed is going to hike rates sometimes this year. This time, it will be one of the things that will fuel a dollar rise," predicted Bob Cortright, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson senior proprietary trader for foreign exchange.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is meeting on Wednesday amid expectations it will keep rates unchanged.

"The U.S. economy is roaring ahead, it's the best place in the world to place your money," Cortight added. "People will come for higher U.S. yields. Taking out the 1994 high won't be a problem. We're going to 1.80 marks. I won't rule out 1.85."
Dollar/mark on Wednesday set a fresh 40-month high at 1.7538 -- 1-1/2 pfennigs short of the 1994's high at 1.7686 set four days after the Fed embarked on stringent tightening.

The rapid-fire rate hikes ended speculative buying of U.S. Treasuries, triggering a capital exodus that caused -- and was exacerbated by -- a constantly weakening dollar that fell to a record low of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995.

Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell noted "the December fed funds rate futures has priced in more than a 25-basis-point tightening" this year which would support -- not undermine -- U.S. markets and the dollar.

Chandler noted low interest-rate countries are more vulnerable to major currency swings because of capital flight tied to the end of carry trades -- or borrowing funds at low rates to park the money in high-yielders abroad.
"In 1994, the U.S. was a low-interest-rate country. This is no longer the case. I do not see any meltdown like in 1994," Chandler said. "Japan and Switzerland are the floor."

If dollar/mark passes 1994's high of 1.7686, the next high of 1.83500 goes back to August 1991, a period marked by a currency crisis in Europe and sudden realization for the need of sharply lower U.S. interest rates.

Bank Brussels Lambert vice president Andrew Hodge said the dollar/mark volatility of August 1991, a near-14-pfennig range with a 1.8350 top, reflected expectations of aggressive Fed easing -- the reverse picture of Fed policy in 1994.
"Now, U.S. markets are underestimating the strength of the U.S. economy and we are looking at a little Fed tightening which makes it a good time to buy dollars," Hodge noted.
"We're looking at highs, at least on a daily basis, going back to 1991. I don't know if it's a useful game to play. But you'd better play it if everybody else plays it," Hodge added.

I.D.E.A. senior currency startegist David Durrant agreed the dollar is helped by a relatively stable Fed outlook while major U.S. interest rate moves -- whether tightenig or easing -- ended up hurting the U.S. unit.
"It's a little tightening expectations, not the kind of Fed ratcheting with the repercussions through the Treasury market that pushed the dollar around in 1994," Durrant said.

"There is no case for selling Treasuries this time, for any given reason, even if you expect a tightening soon," Durrant added. "U.S. stocks have an amazing resilience because of the zillions of dollars pouring into stock mutual funds."

All analysts agreed the other key factor in the dollar/mark rally is the German mark's loss of safe-haven currency status in Europe due to prospects of diluted criteria for the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"There is no guarantee that we are going to have a Bundesbank-type policy backing the euro with the European Central Bank," Bank Brussels Lambert's Hodge said of the planned 1999 EMU launch.
